{"path":"effect_gouraud_shaded_cube_anthropic-claude-sonnet-5_01.html","edit_description":"
Create a complete, self-contained, single HTML file implementing a realtime Gouraud-shaded rotating 3D cube rendered with Canvas 2D only (no WebGL, no external libraries, no external assets). Requirements:

STRUCTURE
- Single .html file with inline <style> and inline <script>. No external requests.
- Full-window <canvas> (resizes with window, handle 'resize' event, account for devicePixelRatio for crisp rendering).
- Dark background page. Small HUD overlay (absolute positioned div) showing: "FPS: N", current mode (Wireframe ON/OFF), Paused ON/OFF, and short key hints ("W: wireframe  P: pause").

3D PIPELINE (implement manually, no library)
- Define cube geometry as 8 vertices (local space, centered at origin, e.g. +-1 on each axis) and 6 quad faces defined by vertex index lists in consistent winding order, plus a distinct RGB base color per face so faces are visually distinguishable.
- Split every quad face into 2 triangles (so 12 triangles total), each triangle carrying references to its 3 vertex indices and the parent face color.
- Rotation: implement 3x3 (or 4x4, your choice, but keep it minimal — 3x3 rotation matrices are enough since we only rotate, no translation of the model itself before rotation) rotation matrices for X, Y, Z axes as plain functions building matrices from cos/sin of angles, and a function to multiply a vertex (vec3) by a matrix. Compose rotations around all three axes with independent, slowly changing angles driven by elapsed time (each axis a different speed) so the rotation is continuous and not paused-looking.
- Camera / world transform: after rotating, translate the model along Z away from the camera (e.g. z += 5) so it sits in front of the perspective projection.
- Perspective projection: implement a standard perspective divide, e.g. screenX = centerX + (x * focalLength / z) * scale, screenY = centerY + (y * focalLength / z) * scale, using a focal length / fov constant. Keep projected 2D coordinates AND keep the camera-space z (post-rotation, post-translation, pre-projection) per vertex for depth sorting and lighting.
- Backface culling: for each triangle, compute the face normal via cross product of two edge vectors in camera space (using the triangle's rotated vertices, consistent winding), and a view vector from the triangle (e.g. its centroid) to the camera (origin, since camera is at origin looking down +z or -z — be consistent with your projection sign convention). Cull (skip rendering) triangles whose normal points away from the camera (dot(normal, viewDir) <= 0, adjust sign to match your winding so the cube renders correctly with the front-facing sides visible and back faces removed).
- Painter's algorithm: after culling, sort remaining triangles back-to-front by average camera-space z (or centroid z) before rasterizing, so nearer triangles draw over farther ones (simple depth handling appropriate for a convex cube with backface culling — no z-buffer needed, but implement the sort for correctness with the moving light and viewing angle).

LIGHTING (Lambertian, per-vertex -> Gouraud)
- Maintain a light position in world/camera space that MOVES over time (e.g. orbits around the cube on a circle in the XZ or XY plane as a function of elapsed time, so lighting visibly sweeps across the cube's faces as it rotates and as the light moves).
- Also add a small ambient term (e.g. 0.15-0.2) so unlit faces are not pure black.
- For each vertex of each visible triangle, compute a vertex normal. Since this is a flat-shaded-per-face cube, approximate a smooth vertex normal per face using the FACE normal (the same normal used for culling) for every vertex of that face — this still allows genuine Gouraud interpolation across the triangle because the light DIRECTION vector differs per vertex position (per-vertex light-to-vertex vector), even though the surface normal is constant across the face; compute per-vertex Lambert term as max(0, dot(faceNormal, normalize(lightPos - vertexPosCameraSpace))) * lightIntensity + ambient, then multiply the face's base RGB color by that scalar (clamped to [0,1] per channel after scaling, clamp final 0-255) to get a final per-vertex shaded color (r,g,b).
- This produces 3 different (r,g,b) shaded-color vertices per triangle (because vertex positions differ even though normal is shared), enabling real color interpolation across the triangle face, not flat single-color fill.

RASTERIZATION / GOURAUD SHADING (must be implemented manually — do NOT use canvas fillStyle gradients as a shortcut for the whole triangle; do real scanline or barycentric interpolation)
- Implement a function to rasterize a single triangle with per-vertex colors using standard techniques: either (a) a scanline triangle rasterizer that sorts the 3 projected 2D vertices by Y, splits into a flat-top/flat-bottom pair, and linearly interpolates x and color (r,g,b) per scanline row using edge interpolation factors, drawing each horizontal span pixel run via a single putImageData-backed pixel buffer OR many small fillRect(1px height) calls, OR (b) a barycentric-coordinate approach: compute the triangle's 2D bounding box, iterate over each pixel in the box, compute barycentric weights (w0, w1, w2) relative to the 3 projected vertices, skip pixels outside the triangle (any weight <0), and interpolate the per-vertex colors using the barycentric weights to get the final pixel color, setting it into an ImageData buffer for performance.
- Use a single reusable ImageData / Uint8ClampedArray sized to the canvas, clear it each frame (fill with background color), draw all visible sorted triangles into it via the rasterizer, then putImageData once per frame for performance (avoid thousands of fillRect calls if possible, though a simple scanline-with-fillRect fallback is acceptable if performance stays smooth for a single small cube — prefer the ImageData buffer approach for quality).
- If wireframe mode is toggled on, skip the filled rasterization and instead just stroke the 3 edges of every visible triangle with a thin light-colored line (e.g. using canvas lineTo strokes), still respecting backface culling and depth sort, but of course no fill color interpolation is needed for wireframe mode (edges can be a single stroke color, optionally still using canvas 2D path stroking rather than the pixel buffer for this mode).

INTERACTION
- 'W' key toggles wireframe mode on/off.
- 'P' key toggles pause on/off (freezes rotation angle and light angle progression; the rendered frame stays static while paused, but you should still update the HUD text to show "Paused: ON").
- Use requestAnimationFrame for the render loop; track elapsed time via performance.now() delta, only advance rotation/light angles when not paused.
- Compute and display FPS: keep a rolling measurement (e.g. update the displayed FPS value roughly once per second, or an exponential moving average of 1000/deltaMs) — show as an integer in the HUD.

CODE QUALITY
- Plain vanilla JS (ES6 ok), no imports, no CDN scripts, no frameworks.
- Reasonably commented sections: geometry setup, matrix/vector math helpers, projection, lighting, rasterizer, animation loop, input handling.
- Make sure the whole thing runs by simply opening the HTML file in a browser (file:// is fine, no build step, no fetch calls).
- Keep everything (HTML, CSS, JS) in this one file.
"}
